subject: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies

messages.author: 63cc02caac0434cf
messages.subject: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
parts:
Hi, 

This is a follow up to my post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/nimble-users/b8G-1MtTm-c/smrwlsTUBAAJ which was about how to sum a parameter vector across neighbors.

The solution we came up with was to use a Nimble function,

nei_sum <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(param = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {
    
    return(sum(param[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]]))
    
    returnType(double(0))
    
  })

Here, param is the parameter vector, adj is a vector of neighbors, count is the starting index and num is the number of neighbors. This works computationally but creates many unnecessary dependencies in the model and probably greatly increases run time. 

Take this as a simple example. Say we have a parameter vector S[1:N] and we create the nodes 

for(i in 1:N){
   neisum[i] <-  nei_sum(param=S[1:N],adj=adj[1:L],count=count[1:N],num=num[1:N],i=i)
}

neisum[i] is the sum of S[1:N] across the neighbors of i. Consider i=1 and suppose that locations 2 and 5 are neighbors of location 1. Then neisum[1] is equivalent to 

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5] 

The problem is that with the correct dependency structure only S[2] and S[5] should have neisum[1] as a dependency. However, with the nei_sum function all the S have neisum[1] as a dependency. So, for example, if you update S[6] it will update neisum[1] even though in reality there is no connection. Obviously, in very large models this could greatly increase the run time and have ripple effects if there are further dependencies of the neisum[i]s. 

So far I can only think of two solutions which are not really satisfactory. First you could just write out each sum manually like so, 

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
neisum[2] <- .... 
.
.
.
neisum[N] <- ... 

I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?

A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.  

Can anyone think of a better solution?

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
parts:
Hi Dirk,

Setting aside issues of cyclic graphs (which won't work), here are a couple of other inelegant but perhaps slightly more appealing solutions to sum over neighbor sets without creating unnecessary dependencies.

Option 1:
If you can break the neighbor indices into sets grouped by number of neighbors, and if there aren't ever a huge number of neighbors, you could do something like this
# neighbor_indices[i, j] is the jth neighbor of cell i
# two neighbors:
for(i in 1:number_of_cells_with_two_neighbors)  {
  neisum[ two_neighbor_cells[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[ three_neighbor_cells[i], 1] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 2] ]
} 

# three neighbors:
for(i in 1:number_of_cells_with_three_neighbors)  {
  neisum[ three_neighbor_cells[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[ three_neighbor_cells[i], 1] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 2] ] + S[ neighbor_indices[three_neighbor_cells[i], 3] ]
} 
# etc.

# Option 2:
for(i in 1:num_cells) {
  reisum[i, num_neighbors[i] ] <- S[ neighbor_indices[i, num_neighbors[i] ] ]
  for(j in 2:num_neighbors[i]) {
     neisum[i, j-1] <- neisum[i, j] + S[ neighbor_indices[i, j-1] ]
  }
}
# Result is that neisum[i, j] is the sum from j to the last neighbor of cell 1, so neisum[i, 1] is the sum of all neighbors of cell i

Option 1 uses more code but creates fewer dependencies in the model graph.
Option 2 uses less code but creates sequences of deterministic dependencies that, if they are very long, can bog down some steps, particularly conjugacy checking.  If you don't need conjugacy checking, you can set useConjugacy=FALSE in configureMCMC.

I haven't tested these.  It's highly possible I glitched the indexing, but I hope the ideas are clear.

This is an interesting problem for the design of the system - something to think about.

-Perry

messages.author: 63cc02caac0434cf
messages.subject: Re: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
parts:
Thanks Perry! 

Your second solution worked really well. I used a slightly different coding 

      Snei[num[i],i] <- S[adj[count[i]]]
      for(j in 2:num[i]){
        Snei[num[i]-j+1,i] <- Snei[num[i]-j+2,i] + S[adj[count[i]+j-1]]
      }

Only thing I am confused about is how the backward indexing works? In some cases num[i]=1 so the for loop would be for(j in 2:1). I am guessing it just doesn't run the loop in these cases since it seemed to return the correct sum. 

This reduced the run time of my model from 6.5 hours to 1 hour so it is a massive improvement! 

About the cyclical graph, I think that could be a really great use case for this. My understanding is that some models are best specified with a cyclical graph, like the Leroux model, although it does not always lead to a valid model. It would be interesting if you could specify a cyclical graph and Nimble would be able to decide if it was valid and form some samplers, maybe even using pseudo likelihood if necessary. Then you could fit general markov random field models in Nimble. See this paper for a good example of the type of models I am talking about, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/env.2427.  

Although in my case I do not have a cyclical graph. I have another important use case of lagged dependence in a spatio-temporal model. I think Andrew Lawson talked about this in the previous thread and he has some papers on it.

messages.subject: Re: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
parts:
Glad it worked!

That's a good point about the backward indexing.  I think a "2:1" case will not be included.  I think you could check with model$getDependencies("S[3]") if, for example, S[3] is the single neighbor in a case with num[i] = 1.

Thanks for the paper link.  The one thoroughly developed case of a cyclic graph in nimble is support for CAR models.  It's not clear to me how well one could automate handling of cyclic graphs, but I wonder if there is an intermediate (in generality) way to support them with some boost of information from the analyst.

-Perry

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors: Removing Unnecessary Dependencies
parts:
Everyone don't forget the nimble system option: "processBackwardsModelIndexRanges"

The default value for this option is FALSE.  That means "backwards" indexing ranges in BUGS model definitions won't create any nodes (e.g., for(i in 5:1) x[i] ~ ....)

If you set:
nimbleOptions(processBackwardsModelIndexRanges = TRUE)

prior to model building, then the example above would in fact create 5 nodes: x[1], x[2], ... x[5].

-Perry

I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?

A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.  

Can anyone think of a better solution?

parts:
Thanks Daniel, so the model was working as intended. 

Thanks for your comments Perry. I am not an expert on markov random fields, but I have read some papers on the topic. Here is one way you could form samplers for arbitrary cyclical graphs. 

So, say you have a vector of nodes x=(x_1,...,x_N) that the user defines a cyclical graph over. This means the user specifies p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda) for i=1,...,N where lambda is some hyper parameters. Here x_(-i) are all x but x_i. Then the full conditional for x_i is p(x_i | x_(-i),  lambda, theta, y) which is proportional to p(y_i | x_i, theta)*p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda). Therefore, you can sample x_i one at a time using MH/binary/categorical etc. samplers, depending on the type of node. 

Sampling lambda though is the bigger issue. p(lambda | x, theta, y) is proportional to p(x | lambda)*p(lambda) but p(x | lambda) might not even exist like with the CAR model. I think there are 3 cases to consider and this is where user input can come in. First in some proper Gaussian models you can go from  p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda) to p(x | lambda) using formulas. Secondly for improper models, I think you need to consider a sensible posterior kernel for lambda, maybe the user can supply this. Finally in some models, like potts model, p(x|lambda) exists but is too difficult to compute. In this case you can use pseudo likelihood, p(x|lambda) is substituted with the product of  p(x_i | x_(-i), lambda). 

Again I am by no means an expert on this topic so if anyone has a better idea how to implement something like this please contribute.
On Tuesday, June 23, 2020 at 5:15:02 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:
Thanks Daniel!
On Tue, Jun 23, 2020 at 1:54 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:

Everyone don't forget the nimble system option: "processBackwardsModelIndexRanges"

The default value for this option is FALSE.  That means "backwards" indexing ranges in BUGS model definitions won't create any nodes (e.g., for(i in 5:1) x[i] ~ ....)

If you set:
nimbleOptions(processBackwardsModelIndexRanges = TRUE)

prior to model building, then the example above would in fact create 5 nodes: x[1], x[2], ... x[5].
On Tue, Jun 23, 2020 at 4:35 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

Glad it worked!

That's a good point about the backward indexing.  I think a "2:1" case will not be included.  I think you could check with model$getDependencies("S[3]") if, for example, S[3] is the single neighbor in a case with num[i] = 1.

Thanks for the paper link.  The one thoroughly developed case of a cyclic graph in nimble is support for CAR models.  It's not clear to me how well one could automate handling of cyclic graphs, but I wonder if there is an intermediate (in generality) way to support them with some boost of information from the analyst.

-Perry
On Tue, Jun 23, 2020 at 12:59 PM Dirk Douwes-Schultz <dirkdouw...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks Perry! 

Your second solution worked really well. I used a slightly different coding 

      Snei[num[i],i] <- S[adj[count[i]]]
      for(j in 2:num[i]){
        Snei[num[i]-j+1,i] <- Snei[num[i]-j+2,i] + S[adj[count[i]+j-1]]

Only thing I am confused about is how the backward indexing works? In some cases num[i]=1 so the for loop would be for(j in 2:1). I am guessing it just doesn't run the loop in these cases since it seemed to return the correct sum. 

This reduced the run time of my model from 6.5 hours to 1 hour so it is a massive improvement! 

About the cyclical graph, I think that could be a really great use case for this. My understanding is that some models are best specified with a cyclical graph, like the Leroux model, although it does not always lead to a valid model. It would be interesting if you could specify a cyclical graph and Nimble would be able to decide if it was valid and form some samplers, maybe even using pseudo likelihood if necessary. Then you could fit general markov random field models in Nimble. See this paper for a good example of the type of models I am talking about, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/env.2427.  

Although in my case I do not have a cyclical graph. I have another important use case of lagged dependence in a spatio-temporal model. I think Andrew Lawson talked about this in the previous thread and he has some papers on it. 



On Saturday, June 20, 2020 at 12:44:35 PM UTC-4, Dirk Douwes-Schultz wrote:
Hi, 

This is a follow up to my post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/nimble-users/b8G-1MtTm-c/smrwlsTUBAAJ which was about how to sum a parameter vector across neighbors.

The solution we came up with was to use a Nimble function,

nei_sum <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(param = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {
    
    return(sum(param[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]]))
    
    returnType(double(0))
    
  })

Here, param is the parameter vector, adj is a vector of neighbors, count is the starting index and num is the number of neighbors. This works computationally but creates many unnecessary dependencies in the model and probably greatly increases run time. 

Take this as a simple example. Say we have a parameter vector S[1:N] and we create the nodes 

for(i in 1:N){
   neisum[i] <-  nei_sum(param=S[1:N],adj=adj[1:L],count=count[1:N],num=num[1:N],i=i)
}

neisum[i] is the sum of S[1:N] across the neighbors of i. Consider i=1 and suppose that locations 2 and 5 are neighbors of location 1. Then neisum[1] is equivalent to 

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5] 

The problem is that with the correct dependency structure only S[2] and S[5] should have neisum[1] as a dependency. However, with the nei_sum function all the S have neisum[1] as a dependency. So, for example, if you update S[6] it will update neisum[1] even though in reality there is no connection. Obviously, in very large models this could greatly increase the run time and have ripple effects if there are further dependencies of the neisum[i]s. 

So far I can only think of two solutions which are not really satisfactory. First you could just write out each sum manually like so, 

neisum[1] <- S[2]+S[5]
neisum[2] <- .... 
.
.
.
neisum[N] <- ... 

I think this should work well it is just a bit janky to write it line by line. In my case I have 160 locations so its 160 lines added to the model. Imagine if you have 1000s of locations?

A second solution would be to rewrite all the samplers that update S and fix the dependencies in the setup. I do not really like this solution either but it would scale better with the number of locations.  

Can anyone think of a better solution?
